PEPTIDE EDUCATION

Peptide basics, without the jargon

A beginner-friendly guide explaining what peptides are, how researchers describe them, and the basic terms customers commonly see.

View catalog

Peptide Education

Peptide terminology can be technical. Select a question below for a clear, beginner-friendly explanation of the underlying research concepts.

What is a peptide?

A peptide is a small chain of amino acids.

Amino acids are the building blocks your body uses to make proteins. Peptides are smaller than proteins and often act like messengers inside the body.

The easiest way to understand it: A peptide is like a text message that tells certain cells in the body what job to perform.

Different peptides send different messages.

Are all peptides the same?

No. The word “peptide” describes a type of molecule, not one specific product or effect.

Different peptides may be researched for different purposes, including:

  • Metabolism and appetite signaling
  • Recovery and tissue repair
  • Sleep and relaxation
  • Skin and hair health
  • Hormone signaling
  • Immune system research
  • Cognitive and neurological research

Each peptide should be researched individually because they do not all work the same way.

Are peptides steroids?

No. Peptides and anabolic steroids are completely different types of compounds.

Steroids usually interact with hormone receptors and can directly change hormone activity. Peptides are generally smaller signaling molecules that communicate with cells and receptors.

A simple comparison: Steroids are like adding more fuel to an engine. Peptides are more like sending instructions to the engine’s computer.

This is only a basic comparison, but it helps explain the difference.

Are peptides naturally found in the body?

Many peptides occur naturally in the human body.

Examples include insulin, glucagon, oxytocin and several hormones involved in appetite, digestion, growth and recovery.

Some research peptides are made in laboratories to copy or study signals that naturally occur in the body.

Do peptides work immediately?

Not necessarily.

Peptides are not usually like caffeine or a pain reliever where a person immediately feels an effect.

The research timeline depends on the specific peptide, the purpose of the research and the biological response being studied. Some signals may act quickly, while other effects may take longer to observe.

Does a higher amount mean better results?

No. More is not always better.

Peptides interact with specific receptors and biological pathways. Using a larger amount does not automatically create a stronger or better response and may increase risk.

Are peptides approved medications?

Some peptide-based medications are approved for specific medical conditions.

Many products commonly called “research peptides” are not approved by the FDA for human use.

Each product should be evaluated separately. Customers should never assume that every peptide has been proven safe or effective.

What does “research use only” mean?

“Research use only” means the product is sold for laboratory, analytical or educational research purposes.

It is not being sold as a medication, dietary supplement or treatment for a medical condition.

Why are peptides sold as a powder?

Many peptides are unstable when stored in liquid for long periods.

For this reason, they are often freeze-dried into a powder through a process called lyophilization. This helps improve stability during storage and transportation.

What does lyophilized mean?

Lyophilized simply means freeze-dried.

The moisture has been removed from the product, leaving a dry powder inside the vial.

Why does the amount of powder look so small?

Peptides are measured in milligrams, which are very small amounts.

A vial may contain the correct labeled amount even when the visible powder looks minimal.

The amount of powder can also appear different depending on the peptide, fillers used during manufacturing and how the product settled during shipping.

Why does the powder sometimes look like a solid puck?

Freeze-dried peptides may appear as a solid puck, loose powder, flakes or a thin layer on the bottom of the vial.

Appearance alone does not determine the amount or quality of the product.

How should research peptides be stored?

Storage requirements can vary by product.

In general, research materials should be protected from excessive heat, direct sunlight, moisture and repeated temperature changes.

Always review the storage information provided for the specific product.

Can peptides treat an injury or medical condition?

This website does not diagnose, treat or provide medical advice.

Research information should not be interpreted as a promise that a product can treat, cure or prevent an injury, disease or medical condition.

Anyone considering treatment for a health concern should speak with a licensed healthcare professional.

Are peptides safe?

Safety depends on the specific peptide, purity, research conditions and many other factors.

The word “peptide” does not automatically mean safe, natural or risk-free.

Some peptides have extensive medical research, while others have limited human data.

What should I research before selecting a peptide?

Before selecting a product, understand:

  • What the peptide is
  • What pathway or receptor it interacts with
  • What it is being researched for
  • Whether human studies are available
  • Potential side effects and risks
  • Whether it is approved for medical use
  • Proper storage requirements

Do not choose a peptide based only on social media claims or before-and-after pictures.

Important Notice

The information on this website is provided for general education and research purposes only.

Products labeled for research use are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease and are not intended for human consumption.

Nothing on this website should be considered medical advice.

Educational information only

This guide explains general concepts and research terminology. It is not medical advice, a treatment recommendation, or directions for personal use.

Clinical research

Tirzepatide

Blood Sugar & Weight Regulation

Tirzepatide activates two hormone pathways called GIP and GLP-1. In simple terms, these signals help the body respond to food by improving insulin release when glucose is high, reducing hunger, and slowing how quickly food leaves the stomach. Researchers study how those effects influence blood sugar, appetite, and body weight.

Research questions
Glucose regulationAppetite signalingInsulin responseBody-weight research
Why researchers care

The purpose is to measure changes in clearly defined biological markers and compare them with an appropriate control—not to assume that an effect seen in a cell or animal automatically applies to people.

Clinical research

Retatrutide

Weight & Energy Metabolism

Retatrutide activates GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors. The GLP-1 and GIP signals are studied for appetite, fullness, digestion, and insulin response. The glucagon pathway is also being studied for its effect on how the body uses stored energy. Researchers are testing whether combining all three signals can create a broader effect on body weight and metabolic health.

Research questions
Appetite and fullnessGastric emptyingEnergy expenditureMetabolic health
Why researchers care

The purpose is to measure changes in clearly defined biological markers and compare them with an appropriate control—not to assume that an effect seen in a cell or animal automatically applies to people.

Cagrilintide

Appetite & Fullness Signaling

Cagrilintide is designed to act like amylin, a hormone released after eating. Amylin helps tell the brain that enough food has been consumed and also affects how quickly food moves through the stomach. Researchers study whether a longer-lasting amylin signal can reduce food intake and support body-weight research.

Research questions
SatietyFood intakeGastric emptyingBody-weight research

MOTS-c

Cellular Energy & Metabolism

MOTS-c is a small peptide produced from mitochondrial genetic material. Mitochondria are the parts of cells that help turn nutrients into usable energy. Researchers are studying whether MOTS-c helps cells adapt to metabolic stress and influences glucose use, energy balance, and age-related changes. Most evidence remains early or preclinical.

Tesamorelin

Growth-Hormone Signaling

Tesamorelin is a laboratory-made version of growth hormone-releasing hormone. Instead of being growth hormone itself, it signals the pituitary gland to release more of the body’s own growth hormone. Researchers study its effects on growth-hormone patterns, IGF-1, fat distribution, and body composition.

Growth-hormone releaseIGF-1 signalingVisceral-fat researchBody composition

Established biological pathway

HGH

Growth-Hormone Biology

Human growth hormone is a signaling protein made by the pituitary gland. Researchers use it to study growth, protein production, bone turnover, tissue development, and the way the body divides nutrients between fat and lean tissue. The purpose of this research is to better understand normal and abnormal growth-hormone physiology.

Research questions
Growth physiologyProtein synthesisBone metabolismBody composition
Why researchers care

IGF-1 LR3

Cell Growth & IGF Signaling

IGF-1 LR3 is a modified form of insulin-like growth factor 1 designed to remain active longer in laboratory models. IGF-1 is part of the growth-hormone pathway and sends signals related to cell growth, protein production, and nutrient use. Researchers use LR3 mainly to examine IGF receptor signaling in cell and animal studies; it is not the same as approved medical IGF-1 products.

Research questions
IGF-1 receptor signalingCell growthProtein synthesisNutrient metabolism

NAD+

Cellular Energy & Repair Chemistry

NAD+ is a molecule found in every living cell. It helps enzymes turn food into cellular energy and also participates in DNA repair and stress-response pathways. Researchers study how NAD+ levels change with aging, illness, and metabolic stress, and whether changing NAD+ availability alters those processes.

Research questions
Cellular energyDNA-repair enzymesRedox biologyAging research

Clomiphene is a selective estrogen-receptor modulator. Researchers study how its tissue-dependent estrogen-receptor activity changes hypothalamic and pituitary feedback and influences luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone signaling.

Research questions
Estrogen receptorsHypothalamic feedbackLH and FSH signalingReproductive endocrinology

Turinabol

Androgen-Receptor & Metabolism Research

Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone, commonly called Oral Turinabol, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid. Research has focused on androgen-receptor activity, protein and nitrogen metabolism, pharmacokinetics, metabolite identification, and anti-doping detection.

Androgen receptorProtein metabolismPharmacokineticsMetabolite detection

Nolvadex

Selective Estrogen-Receptor Modulation

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen-receptor modulator with tissue-specific agonist and antagonist effects. Research examines estrogen-receptor signaling, gene transcription, endocrine feedback, breast-tissue biology, and resistance mechanisms.

Estrogen receptorsGene transcriptionEndocrine feedbackResistance pathways

Established hormone research

T3

Thyroid-Hormone Receptor Signaling

Triiodothyronine, commonly called T3, is an active thyroid hormone. Researchers study its binding to nuclear thyroid-hormone receptors and its effects on gene expression, energy expenditure, thermogenesis, cardiovascular signaling, and tissue development.

Thyroid receptorsGene expressionEnergy metabolismThermogenesis

Investigational research

RAD140

Selective Androgen-Receptor Signaling

RAD140, also called testolone, is an investigational selective androgen receptor modulator. Laboratory research examines how it binds and activates androgen receptors and how that signaling may affect skeletal muscle, bone, reproductive tissues, hormone markers, lipids, liver enzymes, and other safety endpoints.

Research questions
Androgen receptorMuscle and bone modelsHormone markersSafety monitoring

Androgen-Receptor & Metabolism Research

Winstrol is the trade name commonly associated with stanozolol, a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid. Research has examined androgen-receptor activity, protein and nitrogen metabolism, blood-lipid changes, liver metabolism, pharmacokinetics, metabolite identification, and analytical detection.

Early preclinical research

YK-11

Androgen-Receptor & Myostatin-Pathway Models

YK-11 is an investigational steroidal compound studied mainly in cell-based models. Researchers have examined androgen-receptor signaling and reported effects involving follistatin expression and muscle-cell differentiation. Published evidence is limited, and its pharmacology and safety profile remain poorly characterized.

Dapoxetine

Serotonin-Transporter Signaling

Dapoxetine is a short-acting selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Researchers study its binding to the serotonin transporter, its effects on synaptic serotonin signaling, its rapid absorption and elimination, neurobehavioral endpoints, and cardiovascular and other safety markers.

Anavar

Oxandrolone Androgen-Receptor Research

Anavar is the trade name commonly associated with oxandrolone, a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid. Research has examined androgen-receptor signaling, protein metabolism, nitrogen balance, body-composition endpoints, recovery from catabolic states, and changes in liver and lipid markers.
